title: Emor: one law (Leviticus 24:22)
hookLine: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born"

lines: AN ISRAELITE MOTHER, AN EGYPTIAN FATHER.
DOES THE LAW APPLY TO HIM?
cards: A fight in the camp. Near the end of Emor, the long list of laws suddenly breaks into a story. One of the men has an Israelite mother, Shelomith, daughter of Dibri, from the tribe of Dan, and an Egyptian father.
In the quarrel, he curses the Name of God. Half-insider, half-outsider: does the law even apply to someone like him? Nobody is sure.
They put him in custody and wait for an answer.

teach.h: A STORY BREAKS INTO THE LAWS.
teach.b: The verdict comes, and it's severe, as the Torah's punishments for cursing God are. Then the text widens from this one man to everyone, with laws about harming people and animals.
In the middle sits the answer to the question that started it all.
In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for the home-born; for I am the LORD your God."

The Hebrew word for stranger is ger, someone living among the people who wasn't born into them. The same law protects them and binds them: no special harshness for the outsider, no special leniency for the insider.

teach.h: GER: THE ONE WHO LIVES AMONG YOU.
teach.b: At the very first Passover, in Exodus, the Torah already set down one law for the home-born and for the stranger who lives among you.

teach.h: ONE LAW SINCE THE FIRST PASSOVER.
teach.b: Now, at a moment of real doubt, it says it again. The hard verse nearby gets the same treatment. This passage has the line people quote as an eye for an eye.
The rabbis of the Talmud ruled that it means payment, the value of an eye, not an actual eye, and argued for it at length.
Rabbinic law followed that ruling, and applied it, for the same injury, to everyone. One measure, for the ger and the home-born alike. And it started with a man nobody was sure about.

how: Jewish law and teaching repeatedly cite the Torah's command not to wrong the ger, the stranger, and the Passover seder's memory of being strangers in Egypt is often linked to welcoming outsiders.

games.q: a man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father is in custody. the people aren't sure whether the law applies to him. what does the Torah answer?
o: a separate law for people like him.
one manner of law for the stranger and the home-born.
let him go; the law isn't his.
games.why: one law, for the stranger as for the home-born. the case of one uncertain man becomes a rule for everyone.

practice: Think of someone who's a stranger in a place you know well: the new person at work, the neighbor with an accent, the family that moved in last month.
Notice whether you hold them to a different standard, stricter or more dismissive, than the people you grew up with. Then picture treating them by exactly the same rules as everyone else.
